profile.reading:
This OpenStreetMap point sits roughly 40 feet from a sibling point also named simply STACK Infrastructure at the same San Jose, California location, a distance small enough that the two are best read as two mapped suites in one building rather than two separate facilities. That sibling point's own OpenStreetMap tags place the pair at 2150 Trade Zone Boulevard, San Jose, California 95131, distinguishing a level 0 unit 107 from a level 1 unit 201, and this record is treated here as the second of that pair rather than as an independent duplicate campus entry. The City of San Jose parcel layer returns assessor parcel 244-17-011 at this point, zoned IP for industrial park use, within the North San Jose planning area, with San Jose Water Company as the water provider of record.

STACK Infrastructure, headquartered in Denver, Colorado, publishes its Silicon Valley presence as three campuses spanning 97 acres and 150 megawatts combined, but names and details only two of them on its own site, SVY01 in San Jose at 100 megawatts and SVY02 in Santa Clara at 48 megawatts, a gap of roughly two megawatts against the stated total that most plausibly points to an undisclosed or not yet announced third site rather than to an arithmetic error. For SVY01 specifically, STACK's own page gives 19 acres across four buildings, broken out as SVY01A at 9 megawatts and 140,000 square feet, SVY01B at 32 megawatts and 240,000 square feet, SVY01C at 36 megawatts and 350,000 square feet, and SVY01D at 24 megawatts and 300,000 square feet. STACK's own copy calls the surrounding area among the most constrained development regions in Silicon Valley, language consistent with well documented land, power and water limits on new data center construction across San Jose and neighboring Santa Clara. Nothing in STACK's public materials assigns a suite level address to one of those four lettered buildings, so this record cannot be matched to a specific SVY01A through D building, and no floor area or megawatt figure is written to this row for that reason.

The far better documented power record for this immediate area belongs to a different, adjacent parcel rather than to this building. STACK filed with the California Energy Commission for a small power plant exemption under docket 21-SPPE-02, the STACK Trade Zone Park project, covering separate assessor parcels at 2400 Ringwood Avenue and 1849 Fortune Drive about two tenths of a mile to the west. That filing describes two data center buildings, roughly 522,000 square feet between them, delivering 60 megawatts to information technology equipment, a maximum design electrical load near 90 megawatts on a worst case day, and 91 megawatts of diesel fired standby generation, with Pacific Gas and Electric building a new substation to serve it. The Energy Commission certified that project's environmental review and granted the exemption on April 12, 2023. Those three figures, IT load, utility service, and standby generation, belong to that neighboring parcel and not to this suite, and are recorded here only as regional context.

San Jose requires a special use permit for any data center use and a separate special use permit for large energy projects of 20 megawatts or more, and as of mid 2026 the city was drafting uniform citywide standards covering energy sourcing, water use, air quality and greenhouse gas emissions for such projects. What remains unknown for this specific suite is which SVY01 building it sits within, whether STACK owns or leases the address outright, and any power or floor area figure attributable to it alone.

profile.reading:
This record is a mapped tenant suite, not a building outline and not a campus. Its OpenStreetMap tags place it at 2150 Trade Zone Boulevard, unit 107, on level 0, San Jose, California 95131, with the contributor's own note that the point is somewhere on that floor. A second node about 40 feet away carries the same street address at unit 201 on level 1. The two are two suites in one building rather than two facilities, which is a more useful reading of them than calling them duplicates. Geocoding 2150 Trade Zone Boulevard lands within about 25 feet of the stored coordinates, so the address is sound. The City of San Jose parcel layer returns assessor parcel 244-17-011 at this point, zoned IP for industrial park, in the North San Jose planning area, with San Jose Water Company as the water provider.

STACK Infrastructure is a Denver headquartered wholesale and build to suit operator. It publishes its Silicon Valley market as three campuses across 97 acres totalling 150 MW, but names and details only two, SVY01 in San Jose at 100 MW and SVY02 in Santa Clara at 48 MW. For SVY01 it gives 19 acres, four buildings, and per building figures of 140,000 square feet and 9 MW for SVY01A, 240,000 square feet and 32 MW for SVY01B, 350,000 square feet and 36 MW for SVY01C, and 300,000 square feet and 24 MW for SVY01D. STACK calls all of those capacity without saying whether it means IT load, so this registry records none of them against this row, and in any case a suite level point cannot be matched to one of the four buildings.

The far better record for this block is a state one, and it belongs to the parcel next door. STACK filed with the California Energy Commission for a small power plant exemption under docket 21-SPPE-02, the STACK Trade Zone Park project, covering assessor parcels 244-17-014 and 244-17-009 at 2400 Ringwood Avenue and 1849 Fortune Drive, about two tenths of a mile west of this point. The application describes two data centre buildings, SVY05 at roughly 220,012 square feet and SVY06 at roughly 302,182 square feet, about 522,194 square feet between them, plus a 136,573 square foot advanced manufacturing building, on about 9.8 acres. It states that the data centres will provide 60 megawatts of power to information technology equipment, which the filing labels critical IT. It gives a maximum design electrical load of 90 MW on a worst case day and about 78 MW under average conditions. The backup generating facility it sought the exemption for is rated 91 MW of diesel fired standby in acoustical enclosures. Pacific Gas and Electric would build a new substation and transmission connections, and full buildout water use is put at about 113 acre feet a year. The Energy Commission certified the final environmental impact report and approved the exemption on 12 April 2023.

Those four numbers are worth separating out because they are routinely conflated. The 60 MW is IT load. The 90 MW is the service the site can draw. The 91 MW is diesel that runs only when the grid does not. None of them belongs to this row's building, and the coincidence that 90 and 91 sit a megawatt apart is exactly the kind of thing that produces a wrong capacity in a directory.

San Jose requires a special use permit for data centres, heard at a Planning Director's Hearing, and a special use permit for any large energy use project of 20 megawatts or more. As of June 2026 the city was drafting uniform standards for energy sourcing, water use, air quality and greenhouse gas emissions. What is not known here is which STACK building this suite sits in, whether STACK owns or leases 2150 Trade Zone Boulevard, and any power or floor area figure attributable to this address alone.

reading.body:
Stack Infrastructure, Incorporated operates two facilities in San Jose, California, though detailed power and capacity data for these specific locations are not available in current sources.

Both facilities share an address in the Trade Zone Boulevard area of San Jose. The registry notes these entries likely represent the same underlying company recorded under its formal legal name rather than distinct operators, and flags them for reconciliation with the canonical Stack Infrastructure record that documents the broader operator profile across 22 global locations.

This data covers location and operational presence only. It does not specify the power capacity these San Jose facilities draw from the grid, the square footage of their buildings, or their construction timeline, making it impossible to assess their contribution to regional power demand or AI infrastructure scaling from this record alone.
